summary: This work quantifies how bias-tailored quantum error correction advantages predicted under code-capacity noise are substantially reduced by realistic circuit-level effects, and proposes a bias-filtering CNOT gadget to partially recover these advantages. The authors compare XZZX codes to optimized anisotropic surface codes and find that although anisotropic codes outperform XZZX under code-capacity noise, this advantage disappears under circuit-level noise due to bias degradation in syndrome extraction.
motivation: Understanding whether noise-bias tailoring strategies survive realistic gate-level errors and circuit-level propagation is crucial for practical quantum error correction, since prior works suggested substantial improvements under idealized models but the fundamental question of bias preservation through fault-tolerant circuits remained unresolved.
method: The authors performed circuit-level simulations comparing XZZX and rectangular surface codes with optimized anisotropy under biased dephasing noise ($\eta = p_{\mathrm{bias}}/p_{\mathrm{unbias}}$), and introduced an encoded CNOT gadget that temporarily encodes the target qubit in a $d=3$ repetition code during syndrome extraction to filter non-bias-preserving errors via majority-vote decoding and feed-forward.
result: Under circuit-level noise with $p = 0.003$, the XZZX code achieves comparable performance to optimized anisotropic surface codes, and the bias-filtering CNOT gadget yields a few-percent relative improvement to the XZZX threshold in the regime of high bias ($\eta_{2q} > 50$) and low idle errors ($p_{\mathrm{id}} < p_{2q}/5$), demonstrating that lightweight bias-filtering can recover part of the lost bias-tailoring advantage.
